title: The Top 3 Paradoxes in Project Management
author: The Effective Project Manager
summary: The author argues that three commonly held assumptions about working life are paradoxes that quietly hold project managers back. Working harder and longer is counterproductive compared with sprinting and resting fully; wanting to be heard is best served by speaking less and listening more; and clinging to control through micromanagement lowers the quality of the work. For each, he offers a practical remedy: experiment to find your productive rhythm and negotiate it with the team, practise active listening and speak only with high impact, and delegate according to each person's zone of genius. The piece closes by recommending a scientific-method habit of testing actions against results and staying open to being wrong. It is a compact leadership piece on self-management, listening and delegation, framed for project managers but applicable to anyone leading a team.
points: Rest is treated as part of performance, so the sprint-and-rest rhythm should replace long undifferentiated hours, with the arrangement agreed openly with the team.
Being heard is earned by listening to understand rather than to respond, and by speaking only when the input is high impact.
Micromanagement is framed as a symptom of overconfidence in our own methods rather than a strength.
Delegation works best when each person names a zone of genius, which also shows where to target training.
quotes: The paradox is that working in long, slow efforts is not ideal. At worst it is actually counterproductive.
The resting is just as important as the sprinting, because without rest there is not enough energy to sprint.
The paradox is that if we want to be heard, we actually need to speak less and listen more.
Practice delaying the formulation of a response in your mind. Hold on for longer than you are comfortable.
The surprising, but logical paradox here is that when you only speak with high impact, people will become trained to take what you say more seriously.
Stubbornly clinging to control and directing our team with tiny details may actually be the cause of our problems.
Don’t see delegation as laziness, approach it as strategic growth and a lever on efficiency.
